# Prefix-function thinking

One array does all the work in this section. For a string `s`, the prefix
function is

```text
pi[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of s[0..i]
        that is also a suffix of s[0..i]
```

*Proper* means it cannot be the whole of `s[0..i]`, so `pi[i] < i+1` always.
Storing a length is enough; the two copies are equal by definition, so there is
never a reason to copy the substring itself.

The running example throughout this section is `abacaba`, and the four
questions the section answers are: what is the longest border of each prefix
(problem D's ingredient), where does a pattern occur in a text (problem A),
what are *all* the borders (problem B), and what is the shortest period
(problem C).


```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[font=\small,x=1cm,y=1cm,
  c/.style={draw,minimum width=.9cm,minimum height=.62cm,inner sep=0pt,font=\small},
  hd/.style={draw=none,minimum width=.9cm,minimum height=.5cm,inner sep=0pt,
             font=\scriptsize,text=gray!65},
  pre/.style={c,fill=orange!30},
  suf/.style={c,fill=blue!18},
  fade/.style={c,draw=gray!30,text=gray!35},
  rl/.style={font=\scriptsize,text=gray!65,anchor=east},
  note/.style={font=\scriptsize,anchor=west}]

  \foreach \i in {0,...,6} \node[hd] at (.9*\i,.62) {$\i$};
  \foreach \ch/\i in {a/0,b/1,a/2,c/3,a/4,b/5,a/6} \node[c] at (.9*\i,0) {\texttt{\ch}};
  \foreach \p/\i in {0/0,0/1,1/2,0/3,1/4,2/5,3/6} \node[c,fill=gray!10] at (.9*\i,-.62) {$\p$};
  \node[rl] at (-.52,.62) {$i$};
  \node[rl] at (-.52,0)   {$s$};
  \node[rl] at (-.52,-.62){$\pi$};

  % i = 2
  \foreach \ch/\i/\st in {a/0/pre,b/1/c,a/2/suf,c/3/fade,a/4/fade,b/5/fade,a/6/fade}
    \node[\st] at (.9*\i,-1.72) {\texttt{\ch}};
  \node[note] at (6.1,-1.72) {$\pi[2]=1$\ \ border \texttt{a}};
  % i = 5
  \foreach \ch/\i/\st in {a/0/pre,b/1/pre,a/2/c,c/3/c,a/4/suf,b/5/suf,a/6/fade}
    \node[\st] at (.9*\i,-2.50) {\texttt{\ch}};

    \node[\st] at (.9*\i,-3.28) {\texttt{\ch}};
  \node[note] at (6.1,-3.28) {$\pi[6]=3$\ \ border \texttt{aba}};

    {\textcolor{orange!65!black}{\textbf{prefix copy}} and
     \textcolor{blue!60!black}{\textbf{suffix copy}} must not overlap the

```

## The update rule

Positions are filled left to right. To extend to `s[i]`, take the best border
of the previous prefix, `j = pi[i-1]`, and try to grow it by one character:

```text
j = pi[i-1]
while j > 0 and s[i] != s[j]:
    j = pi[j-1]
if s[i] == s[j]:
    j += 1
pi[i] = j
```

The `while` loop is the only subtle line, and it is not a search. If a border of
length `j` is contradicted, every longer border was already ruled out, so the
longest candidate still alive is the longest border *of that border* — which is
`pi[j-1]`, a value already computed.


```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[font=\small,x=1cm,y=1cm,
  c/.style={draw,minimum width=.9cm,minimum height=.62cm,inner sep=0pt,font=\small},
  b1/.style={c,fill=orange!30},
  b2/.style={c,fill=blue!18},
  pl/.style={c,draw=gray!35,text=gray!45},
  rl/.style={font=\scriptsize,text=gray!65,anchor=east},
  note/.style={font=\scriptsize,anchor=west},
  kb/.style={draw,rounded corners=2pt,minimum width=1.5cm,minimum height=.6cm,
             font=\scriptsize,inner sep=2pt}]

  \foreach \ch/\i/\st in {a/0/b1,b/1/b1,a/2/b1,c/3/pl,a/4/b1,b/5/b1,a/6/b1}
    \node[\st] at (.9*\i,0) {\texttt{\ch}};
  \node[note] at (6.15,0) {longest border of \texttt{abacaba} has length $3$};

  \foreach \ch/\i/\st in {a/0/b2,b/1/pl,a/2/pl,c/3/pl,a/4/pl,b/5/pl,a/6/b2}
    \node[\st] at (.9*\i,-.80) {\texttt{\ch}};
  \node[note] at (6.15,-.80) {the next border has length $1$};

  \node[font=\scriptsize,anchor=north west,align=left,text width=12.6cm] at (-.5,-1.42)
    {A border of a border is again a border, so the border lengths form a chain
     that $\pi$ already stores. Following it enumerates \emph{every} proper
     border, largest first --- that is exactly problem B.};

  \node[kb,fill=orange!25] (k3) at (0.8,-2.72) {$k=3$};
  \node[kb,fill=blue!18]   (k1) at (4.3,-2.72) {$k=1$};
  \node[kb,fill=gray!12]   (k0) at (7.9,-2.72) {$k=0$: stop};
  \draw[->,>=Latex,thick,gray!70] (k3) -- node[above=2pt,font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt]
        {$\pi[2]=1$} (k1);
  \draw[->,>=Latex,thick,gray!70] (k1) -- node[above=2pt,font=\scriptsize,inner sep=1pt]
        {$\pi[0]=0$} (k0);
  \node[font=\scriptsize,text=gray!60,anchor=east] at (-.05,-2.72)
        {$k=\pi[n-1]$:};

  \node[draw=gray!45,rounded corners,fill=gray!4,align=left,font=\scriptsize,
        anchor=north west,inner sep=5pt,text width=12.2cm] at (-.5,-3.75)
    {\textbf{The same chain is the failure link.} While building $\pi$, suppose the
     candidate border has length $j$ and the new character contradicts it. Every
     border longer than $\pi[j-1]$ has already been ruled out, so the longest
     still-possible candidate is $\pi[j-1]$ --- never $0$, and never a fresh
     restart. In \texttt{abacaba} at $i=3$ the candidate is $j=\pi[2]=1$; since
     $s[3]=\texttt{c}\neq s[1]=\texttt{b}$ it falls to $\pi[0]=0$, and
     $\texttt{c}\neq\texttt{a}$ leaves $\pi[3]=0$.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

# KMP matching

To find every occurrence of a pattern `p` of length `m` in a text `t`, run the
prefix function once over

```text
p + separator + t
```

The separator must be a character that cannot appear in either string. Its only
job is to stop a prefix from stretching across the join, which would report
matches that do not exist. If the alphabet is not under your control, do not
concatenate at all; run the matching loop directly against `p` and `t` with the
same fallback rule.

Wherever `pi[i] == m`, the pattern has just finished. Counting back over the
pattern, the separator, and the matched copy gives the 1-based start in the
text:

```text
start = i - 2*m + 1
```


```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[font=\small,x=1cm,y=1cm,
  c/.style={draw,minimum width=.9cm,minimum height=.62cm,inner sep=0pt,font=\small},
  pat/.style={c,fill=orange!28},
  sep/.style={c,fill=gray!30},
  txt/.style={c,fill=blue!12},
  hit/.style={c,fill=green!35,very thick},
  hd/.style={draw=none,minimum width=.9cm,minimum height=.5cm,inner sep=0pt,
             font=\scriptsize,text=gray!65},
  rl/.style={font=\scriptsize,text=gray!65,anchor=east},
  br/.style={decorate,decoration={brace,amplitude=4pt},gray!65}]

  \foreach \i in {0,...,8} \node[hd] at (.9*\i,.66) {$\i$};
  \foreach \ch/\i/\st in {a/0/pat,b/1/pat,a/2/pat,{\#}/3/sep,
                          a/4/txt,b/5/txt,a/6/txt,b/7/txt,a/8/txt}
    \node[\st] at (.9*\i,0) {\texttt{\ch}};
  \foreach \p/\i/\st in {0/0/c,0/1/c,1/2/c,0/3/c,1/4/c,2/5/c,3/6/hit,2/7/c,3/8/hit}
    \node[\st] at (.9*\i,-.66) {$\p$};
  \node[rl] at (-.52,.66) {$i$};
  \node[rl] at (-.52,0)   {char};
  \node[rl] at (-.52,-.66){$\pi$};

  \draw[br] (-.45,.98) -- (2.25,.98)
     node[midway,above=4pt,font=\scriptsize] {pattern, $m=3$};
  \draw[br] (2.55,.98) -- (7.65,.98)
     node[midway,above=4pt,font=\scriptsize] {text};

  \node[font=\scriptsize,text=green!30!black,anchor=north,align=center] at (5.4,-1.02)
    {$\pi=3=m$\\start $=6-6+1=1$};
  \node[font=\scriptsize,text=green!30!black,anchor=north,align=center] at (7.2,-2.05)
    {$\pi=3=m$\\start $=8-6+1=3$};
  \draw[green!45!black,->,>=Latex] (7.2,-1.02) -- (7.2,-1.95);

  \node[draw=gray!45,rounded corners,fill=gray!4,align=left,font=\scriptsize,
        anchor=north west,inner sep=5pt,text width=12.2cm] at (-.6,-3.05)
    {\textbf{Why overlapping matches are not lost.} At $i=7$, just after a full
     match, the candidate is $j=3$. The next character \texttt{b} contradicts it,
     so the loop falls to $\pi[2]=1$ --- the longest border of the pattern ---
     and \texttt{b} matches there, giving $\pi[7]=2$. One more character reaches
     $3$ again at $i=8$. A naive scanner that restarted at $0$ after a match
     would skip the occurrence at position $3$.\\[3pt]
     \textbf{Why the text index never retreats.} Only $j$ moves backwards, and
     it never falls below $0$ while $i$ only advances. Each character raises $j$
     by at most one, so total fallback is bounded by total increase: $O(n)$.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

Overlapping occurrences come out for free, and that is the whole advantage over
naive scanning: after a match the algorithm falls back to the longest border of
the pattern, never to zero, so characters already known to match are never
compared again.

# Borders and periods

## Every border, largest first

The chain in the figure above is also the answer to problem B. The longest
border is `pi[n-1]`; the next is the longest border of *that* prefix, and so on
until the chain reaches zero:

```text
k = pi[n-1]
while k > 0:
    record k
    k = pi[k-1]
```

This produces borders in decreasing order. Reverse the list if the statement
asks for increasing order. For `abacaba` it yields `3, 1`; for `abcabca` it
yields `4, 1`; for `abc` it yields nothing at all.

## The shortest period

A border of length `b` says the string agrees with itself after a shift of
`p = n - b`. That shift is always a valid *overlap* statement, but a period that
tiles the string needs one extra condition:


```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[font=\small,x=1cm,y=1cm,
  c/.style={draw,minimum width=.8cm,minimum height=.58cm,inner sep=0pt,font=\small},
  ov/.style={c,fill=green!30},
  pl/.style={c,fill=white},
  rl/.style={font=\scriptsize,text=gray!65,anchor=east},
  br/.style={decorate,decoration={brace,amplitude=3.5pt,mirror},gray!65},
  bu/.style={decorate,decoration={brace,amplitude=3.5pt},gray!65},
  vd/.style={font=\scriptsize,anchor=west,align=left}]

  % ---------- panel A : ababab ----------
  \node[font=\scriptsize,anchor=west] at (-1.35,1.04)
    {\textbf{\texttt{ababab}}\ \ $n=6$,\ $b=\pi[5]=4$,\ candidate $p=n-b=2$};
  \foreach \ch/\i/\st in {a/0/pl,b/1/pl,a/2/ov,b/3/ov,a/4/ov,b/5/ov}
    \node[\st] at (.8*\i,0) {\texttt{\ch}};
  \foreach \ch/\i/\st in {a/0/ov,b/1/ov,a/2/ov,b/3/ov,a/4/pl,b/5/pl}
    \node[\st] at (.8*\i+1.6,-.62) {\texttt{\ch}};
  \node[rl] at (-.45,0)    {$s$};
  \node[rl] at (-.45,-.62) {$s$ shifted by $p=2$};
  \draw[bu] (-.4,.32) -- (1.2,.32) node[midway,above=3.5pt,font=\scriptsize] {$p=2$};
  \draw[br] (1.2,-.94) -- (4.4,-.94)
     node[midway,below=3.5pt,font=\scriptsize,text=green!30!black]
     {overlap $=$ border \texttt{abab}, length $4$};
  \node[vd,text=green!30!black] at (6.35,-.31)
    {$6 \bmod 2 = 0$\\\textbf{period is $2$}};

  % ---------- panel B : abacaba ----------
  \node[font=\scriptsize,anchor=west] at (-1.35,-1.98)
    {\textbf{\texttt{abacaba}}\ \ $n=7$,\ $b=\pi[6]=3$,\ candidate $p=n-b=4$};
  \foreach \ch/\i/\st in {a/0/pl,b/1/pl,a/2/pl,c/3/pl,a/4/ov,b/5/ov,a/6/ov}
    \node[\st] at (.8*\i,-3.0) {\texttt{\ch}};
  \foreach \ch/\i/\st in {a/0/ov,b/1/ov,a/2/ov,c/3/pl,a/4/pl,b/5/pl,a/6/pl}
    \node[\st] at (.8*\i+3.2,-3.62) {\texttt{\ch}};
  \node[rl] at (-.45,-3.0)  {$s$};
  \node[rl] at (-.45,-3.62) {$s$ shifted by $p=4$};
  \draw[bu] (-.4,-2.68) -- (2.8,-2.68) node[midway,above=3.5pt,font=\scriptsize] {$p=4$};
  \draw[br] (2.8,-3.94) -- (5.2,-3.94)
     node[midway,below=3.5pt,font=\scriptsize,text=green!30!black]
     {overlap $=$ border \texttt{aba}, length $3$};
  \node[vd,text=red!55!black] at (8.75,-3.31)
    {$7 \bmod 4 = 3$\\\textbf{period is $7$}};

  \node[draw=gray!45,rounded corners,fill=gray!4,align=left,font=\scriptsize,
        anchor=north west,inner sep=5pt,text width=12.4cm] at (-1.4,-4.75)
    {A border of length $b$ says the string matches itself after a shift of
     $p=n-b$, so $s[i]=s[i+p]$ wherever both exist. That makes $p$ the shortest
     \emph{candidate} period, and it is always correct as an overlap statement.\\[3pt]
     \textbf{The trap.} It is a \emph{tiling} period only when $p$ divides $n$.
     For \texttt{abacaba} the shift is consistent, but $4$ does not divide $7$:
     the string is not whole copies of \texttt{abac}, so the answer is $n=7$.
     Always test $n \bmod p$ before printing $p$.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

```text
b = pi[n-1]
p = n - b
answer = p if n % p == 0 else n
```

`ababa` is the smallest trap worth memorizing: `pi[4] = 3`, so the candidate is
`5 - 3 = 2`, but `2` does not divide `5` and the answer is `5`.

# Implementation, linearity, and debugging

## Why it is linear

The index `i` never moves backwards. The pointer `j` rises by at most one per
position, so across the whole run it rises at most `n` times. Every iteration of
the `while` loop strictly lowers `j`, and `j` never drops below zero, so the
total number of fallback steps is bounded by the total number of increases.
Both are `O(n)`, which is why a loop that looks quadratic is not.

The loop invariant behind that argument: before position `i` is processed, `j`
is the longest border of `s[0..i-1]` not yet contradicted by the new character.
Each fallback preserves the longest surviving candidate; each success extends it
by exactly one.

## Language notes

**C++.** A `vector<int>` for `pi` is enough. Reserve the combined string once
rather than appending in a loop. Occurrence counts can exceed `int` on
adversarial inputs such as `aaaa...a`, so accumulate in `long long`.

**Python.** Read with `sys.stdin.buffer.read()` and work on `bytes`; indexing a
`bytes` object yields integers and compares faster than slicing strings. Never
build the combined string by repeated `+=` in a loop.

## Tests before trusting a solution

| Case | What it catches |
|---|---|
| pattern longer than text | negative or out-of-range start positions |
| pattern equals text | off-by-one in `i - 2*m + 1` |
| `aba` in `ababa` | a scanner that restarts at zero and loses overlaps |
| `aaaa` in `aaaaa` | the maximal-overlap stress case |
| no occurrence at all | an empty-output path |
| `ababa` for the period | the missing `n % p == 0` divisibility test |
| `abc` for borders | an empty border chain |
| separator present in input | a bogus match across the join |

Useful values to check by hand: `pi("aaaaa") = 0 1 2 3 4`, the proper borders of
`abcabca` are `1` and `4`, and `abacaba` has candidate period `4` but answer `7`.

Run the local reference suite with:

```bash
CP_TARGET=solution python3 sections/43_string_algorithms_i/check.py
```

# Exercises

Use A to get the combined-string indexing and the 1-based start formula right,
B to walk the border chain to exhaustion rather than stopping at the first link,
and C to apply the divisibility test that turns a candidate period into a real
one. Use D as the blind synthesis problem: every prefix needs a count, not just
the whole string, so decide what a failure link contributes to its target before
writing any code. Test a pattern longer than the text, a pattern equal to the
text, overlapping matches, an all-same-character input, and a string with no
border at all.

- A. KMP Occurrences: Print the number and 1-based positions of all occurrences of pattern in text.
- B. All Borders: Print all proper border lengths of a string in increasing order.
- C. Minimal Period: Print the shortest period length if the string is repetitions of a block, otherwise `n`.
- D. Prefix Frequency: For every prefix length, print how many times that prefix occurs as a substring.
